newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS-Mandela seen pledging reform in key speech.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Mandela seen pledging reform in key speech.

text.p: South Africa's rand hit a six-month high against the dollar on Thursday as markets awaited a major speech by President Nelson Mandela.

Political sources said Mandela's address to parliament on Friday was likely to pledge faster implementation of the government's macroeconomic strategy, including privatisation and relaxation of exchange controls.
But the speech was unlikely to contain detailed measures for dismantling exchange controls, which could come in the March 12 budget.

Late on Thursday, officials were still working on the final draft of the 45-minute address which Mandela will deliver at the start of the 1997 session of parliament at 11.00 a.m. (0900 GMT) on Friday.
Sources close to Mandela said his heir apparent, Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, made a major contribution to the speech to be delivered on Friday.

Dealers said expectations of news on easing exchange controls had helped fuel the rand's strong run which took it to a best rate of 4.4570 bid against the dollar on Thursday morning -- a level last seen on August 5, 1996. By the local close the rand had slipped back to around 4.47.
Long bond yields dipped below 15 percent for the first time since September.
Economists say current strong markets represent a good opportunity to ease restrictions stopping residents exporting currency, because any outflows could be matched by strong foreign inflows.
However, most market players still expect a cautious gradualist approach rather than a single "big bang" abolition. The government has said in the past that it favours a step-by-step approach.
Previous Mandela speeches opening parliamentary sessions have been long on general policy goals but short on specific initiatives or plans.

However, Tony Twine of Econometrix noted that after high- level African National Congress policy discussions last month Mbeki had signalled that notable speeches would be made during the opening weeks of parliament.

"So it looks as though it's going to be a slightly more important opening-of-parliament address than we've been used to. That's what the market is now tossing around like a dog plays with a chicken leg," Twine said.

He said no parliamentary opening speech had rivalled in importance that made by F.W. de Klerk in February 1990, when he declared that Mandela would be freed from jail. But Mandela could nevertheless make a major announcement on Friday.
Currency dealers reported heavy dollar selling by overseas and local players while bond investors once again rushed to buy high-yielding South African debt.
The rand has now advanced nearly five percent against the dollar since the start of the year and some seven percent against a trade-weighted basket of currencies.

Analysts say confidence has been restored to South Africa by expectations of a sharply improving trade balance this year which should cut the current account deficit and boost critically low foreign exchange reserves.
A move to relax exchange controls -- signalling the government's own confidence in the country's economic future -- could give markets a further fillip, they said.
Against the current sound economic backdrop there is a growing consensus that the rand should stabilise in 1997, tempting overseas investors back to rand assets once more.
Foreigners snapped up a net 492 million rands ($110 million) of South African bonds on Wednesday, taking net foreign purchases this year to 2.9 billion rand, according to Bond Exchange figures.
